extracted.intended_audience: students preparing for math contests (middle/high school/undergraduate) and their coaches/mentors
extracted.subtask_description: A broad FAQ covering best practices for preparing for math contests: how to start, study strategies, problem selection, write-ups, exam tactics, topic selection, and mindset.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-0. I have zero experience with math contests. Where should I start?
rubrics_metrics.description: For the first several weeks, the most important thing is exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lose your first 50 games as quickly as possible. Do a subset of these: pick up a standard textbook (e.g., AoPS v1 or v2) to learn standard theory; work through past contest problems (no time limit); pick any year and work problems that look interesting; when stuck for an hour, read the solution; repeat until you have a picture of the landscape; learn new contest topics (combinatorics, number theory) beyond school math; aim for deep understanding rather than memorization; expect many unsolvable problems and treat them as learning opportunities; rope friends into learning; stay determined—scoring even 1/3–1/2 is an accomplishment given contest difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-1. How should I prepare for math contests?
rubrics_metrics.description: One-sentence answer: do lots of problems just above your current ability, and spend some time on reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no silver-bullet method; anything reasonable is probably fine. Avoid obvious non-strategies (do nothing, read solutions without trying). The biggest predictor of success is whether you 'think about math in the shower'—i.e., enjoy and do math outside formal sessions and work in the right difficulty range. Reflect on solutions and practice metacognition. For personalized advice, follow the special instructions for study advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-2. Which books/handouts/materials should I use?
rubrics_metrics.description: It probably doesn't matter too much which materials you choose, if you exercise common sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For younger students (AMC/AIME) AoPS Volume 2 is recommended; otherwise choose reasonable books/handouts and avoid over-obsessing about picking a 'perfect' resource. Match material to your level and interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-3. How do I get better at Euclidean geometry?
rubrics_metrics.description: Use general advice and specific materials; learn from multiple handouts and a geometry textbook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Evan's advice, Geoff Smith's advice, and specific handouts by Evan and Yufei Zhao; read Evan's geometry textbook (EGMO) for structured learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-4. Is it possible for me to improve by X amount in Y time if I spend Z hours a week?
rubrics_metrics.description: Predicting improvement is hard; the author 'probably doesn't know much more than you do.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvement prediction is like forecasting the stock market—common sense helps but no precise answer. Expect uncertainty; focus on doing the work rather than precise forecasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-5. How do I learn to write proofs?
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof-writing isn't a mysterious leap from computation; it mainly requires practice and exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read introductory handouts (e.g., 'Intro to Proofs for the Morbidly Curious') and articles; read official solutions to problems you solved; write up solutions and get feedback (mentor, forums); if following a book, consider Rotman's textbook. Graph theory courses can help. For US middle/high school students, participating in programs like the USA Mathematical Talent Search gives practice producing full written solutions over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-6. Am I ready to do X level problems, read book Y, etc.?
rubrics_metrics.description: The correct thing to do is just try it and see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try problems from past X papers or read a chapter from Y to gauge fit. Avoid seeking permission—self-assess by sampling material. Aim for tasks that are neither too easy nor too hard; prefer what's enjoyable.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-7. Should I read X book versus Y book, spend M hours versus N hours per week, etc.?
rubrics_metrics.description: Effect sizes for these choices are small and person-dependent; try both and pick what you like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No definitive universal answer—choose what keeps you engaged. Don't fixate on one 'right' choice; personal preference matters and the difference is often rounding error compared to overall effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-8. How do I make fewer careless errors?
rubrics_metrics.description: Neatness and organization reduce careless mistakes; good scratch work habits help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label each problem on its own page, draw large diagrams, strike out mistakes cleanly, box final answers, don't misread questions or rush. Evan's AIME scratch paper example: structure scratch work to make later review easy. As problem-solving skill increases, careless errors typically decrease.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-9. Should I take the time to write up full solutions to problems I solve in training?
rubrics_metrics.description: It depends, but full write-ups have understated upsides; at minimum write a couple sentences summarizing the main idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Downside: time-consuming. Upsides: consolidates understanding, clarifies moving parts, helps future review. For OTIS, students must record a couple sentences on the main idea. Avoid writing nothing; write especially when solutions have many moving parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-10. Can you solve X problem for me?
rubrics_metrics.description: Probably not; the author will read problems but only solve if quick or known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the problem is familiar or easily seen, the author may outline or link a solution; otherwise messages may be archived due to limited time.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-11. I can’t be bothered to learn directed angles. Can I just use normal angles?
rubrics_metrics.description: You could probably get away with normal angles sometimes, but you should learn directed angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directed angles remove configuration bookkeeping (e.g., x vs 180°-x) and make angle chasing easier once mastered. While deductions for configuration are uncommon, directed angles lead to cleaner and more reliable solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-12. How long should I spend on an olympiad problem before I give up?
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a lower bound (1 hour is a good rule of thumb); for the upper bound use judgment based on progress and enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If making continuous progress or learning, keep going; if stuck for hours with no clue, give up and read the solution. Keep several problems in mind to switch between when stuck. A useful heuristic: give up once the problem stops being fun (after meeting the lower bound).

rubrics_metrics.name: C-13. Do I need to know X topic for math olympiads?
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to the syllabus linked on the beginner page for required topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the contest syllabus to check topic requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-14. In geometry, can I only use synthetic methods and not use coordinates? Or vice versa?
rubrics_metrics.description: Wrong question — always use the tool most suited to the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be versatile: some problems are easier with coordinates, others with synthetic methods. Learn multiple methods and combine perspectives; moving between approaches often yields solutions you wouldn't find using a single method.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-15. On a 3-problem, 4.5-hour exam, should I try all three problems?
rubrics_metrics.description: Yes — due to volatility in problem difficulty, you should at least look at all problems seriously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems can be out of order or personal strengths vary; try all three. One suggested tactic: start by trying problems 3, 2, then 1 for 20 minutes each to force yourself to inspect later problems. Partial marks on late problems are often accessible. Try this on practice exams to see if it suits you.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-16. What grade should I aim to reach X goal by?
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't treat time as an enemy; do your best each year rather than fixating on grade-by-grade quotas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rigid timelines (e.g., specific contest milestones by particular grades); treating time as a friend reduces pressure. Progress depends on work done between now and then, not past missed milestones.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-17. Do I need to make a study plan?
rubrics_metrics.description: You can, but it's not that important; energy management matters more than time management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plans are fine but can waste energy if overcrafted. Better to explore what interests you and follow that energy, unless you are actively avoiding a particular area. If you avoid a topic completely, make a minimal plan to address that gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-18. Do I have to do EVERY problem from X?
rubrics_metrics.description: No.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't feel obligated to exhaust entire collections if it's not useful for your learning; be selective with practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-19. Should I practice with hand-drawn or digital geo diagrams?
rubrics_metrics.description: Do a mix of both; there is no consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hand-drawn practice prevents reliance on generated diagrams during contests; digital (GeoGebra) gives perfect diagrams and helps build intuition and saves time. Balance personal taste and convenience; avoid rigid rules that hamper practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-20. How do I handle stress or pressure?
rubrics_metrics.description: Stress doesn't completely go away and signals that you care; don't misinterpret test difficulty as a personal skill issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that per-year exam difficulty fluctuates widely; if a problem is harder than usual, it's not necessarily your failure. Use small coping tactics (e.g., stand up to calm shaking hands). Don't blame yourself for variations in problem difficulty; this mindset reduces underperformance driven by misattributed causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-21. How should I prepare for the Putnam?
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparation is similar to USAMO but with different topic emphasis and faster time controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Putnam excludes Euclidean geometry but includes abstract/linear algebra, calculus, and some real analysis. Time is faster: six problems in three hours; deciding in five minutes whether to continue on a problem is an important skill. Many top students rely on high-school olympiad training; don't overemphasize Putnam compared to its actual importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-22. For X contest, about how much do I usually need to get Y medal/award?
rubrics_metrics.description: Use available contest statistics (e.g., Evan's problems archive or IMO data) to estimate, but be cautious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can extrapolate values if contest statistics are available. Do not overtrust means/medians because high fluctuation makes averages misleading. Avoid fixed mindsets like 'I need three problems for silver'—contest difficulty variance makes such extrapolations risky.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-23. Since contests get harder over time, should I only work on recent years?
rubrics_metrics.description: No; anything post-2000 is probably fine (as of 2023).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 2000–2010 may be slightly easier on average, and could be better fits for beginners. Don't limit yourself only to the most recent years; a range of years is useful for learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-24. Why are you such a stickler about write-ups? You get 7 points at a contest as long as the solution is correct, right?
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing helps form and improve ideas; separating solving from writing damages both abilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat write-ups as a chance to improve and clean solutions. Writing often changes the content of a solution (restructure, consolidate, catch errors). Poor writing can hide errors and prevent learning. In practice, focus on full marks during contests, but practice write-ups at home to deepen understanding and reduce errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-25. Why don’t you have any olympiad algebra book recommendations?
rubrics_metrics.description: Because 'olympiad algebra' is a hodgepodge of unrelated topics and not a coherent single subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Olympiad algebra includes many disparate things: ad-hoc functional equations, certain inequalities, asymptotic/comparison problems, analysis-like problems, polynomial problems, combinatorial/algebraic crossovers, etc. Better to focus on particular sub-skills or cohesive idea-areas rather than seek a single unified algebra book.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-26. My big important MO is next week, what should I do?
rubrics_metrics.description: Wind down; prioritize rest and a clear head in the last weeks before the contest over cramming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being well-rested and calm is often more beneficial than last-minute practice. Math contest studying should be year-round; last-week intensity increases nervousness and harms scores for many students.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-27. Is it bad if I spend lots of time on practice problems and don’t solve them?
rubrics_metrics.description: It depends: spending hours is fine if you are making progress or learning; if you draw a blank, give up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice is about maximizing experience gained, not fastest solutions. Pushing a method until you understand its failure is valuable (do that in practice, not under timed contest conditions). Long productive sessions can be very educational.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-28. How much of your geometry book do I need to read for IMO?
rubrics_metrics.description: Know chapters 1–3 (basic tools) thoroughly; later chapters are useful but not immediately required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapters 1–3 cover bread-and-butter techniques like angle chasing, power of a point, homothety and are sufficient for many IMO problems. Later chapters open further solution paths and are helpful to study over time; EGMO is close to 'core' material.

rubrics_metrics.name: C-29. Why won’t you give me a straight answer to my question?
rubrics_metrics.description: Because many questions (best resources, probability of success, hours needed) cannot be answered usefully with a single concrete number; such answers can harm more than help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author avoids giving oversimplified numeric answers (e.g., 'M hours per day for N years') because people misuse them (timers, quota thinking). Instead the author suggests focusing on doing the work and not obsessing over a magic number. For personalized advice, follow the posted instructions for study advice.
